Nitra Neolog Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nitra, Slovakia

Not demolished. Nitra is considered the site of Slovakia's oldest Jewish community, first documented in 1113. A formal community re-established itself in the 17th century, growing to over 3,000 residents (roughly a quarter of the population) by the late 19th century. Following the 1868-69 Budapest Congress schism in Hungarian Jewry, about 170 Orthodox families remained separate from a new Neolog congregation formed in 1907; each maintained its own synagogue and cemetery until the Holocaust. Nitra was home to Rabbi Samuel Ungar's renowned yeshiva, one of the last to operate in Nazi-occupied Europe before its 1944 closure; the city's 4,358 Jews in 1940 were mostly murdered in the Holocaust. About 600 survivors returned after the war and reorganized as a single Orthodox community, cleaning and restoring both this cemetery and its Orthodox counterpart, and erecting a Holocaust memorial. In 1963, authorities destroyed most Jewish public buildings in Nitra except the Neolog synagogue; the cemeteries were again vandalized with swastikas after 1989. This Neolog cemetery holds tombstones dated between 1886 and 1987.
